meteorites.name: NWA 6950 (Lunar gabbro)
meteorites.description:
NWA 6950 (Lunar gabbro)
**NWA 6950 is an olivine gabbro belonging to the geologically diverse NWA 773 clan, a group of lunar meteorites that preserves several related but distinct lithologies.** Unlike the fine-grained basalts that dominate many lunar samples, NWA 6950 has a coarse cumulate texture, with olivine, pigeonite, augite and very calcic plagioclase recording crystallization from a magma that cooled slowly beneath the lunar surface. U–Pb dating of baddeleyite and phosphates places its crystallization at approximately **3.13 billion years ago**. Its close mineralogical, chemical and isotopic relationship to other members of the NWA 773 clan supports the interpretation that these rocks represent a related magmatic system rather than simply unrelated lunar basalts. ([Hep Journals][1])

NWA 6950 is particularly valuable because its **shock veins preserve minerals formed under extreme impact conditions**. Recent work identified high-pressure phases including **ringwoodite, tuite and xieite** within these veins. Their presence provides a record of the enormous pressures generated when the meteorite's parent rock was struck by a major lunar impact. The meteorite also contributes to an important question about lunar magmatism: the ~3.1-billion-year ages shared by several NWA 773 clan gabbros coincide with a proposed transition from predominantly **surface-erupted volcanism to more intrusive magmatism** within the Moon. NWA 6950 therefore preserves evidence not only of the Moon's internal magmatic evolution, but also of the extreme impacts that later excavated material from its interior. ([Hep Journals][1])

[1]: https://journal.hep.com.cn/jes/EN/10.1007/s12583-023-1923-0?utm_source=chatgpt.com "Complexity of the NWA 773 Clan: New Evidence from Lunar Olivine Gabbro NWA 6950"

meteorites.name: NWA 16286 (Lunar mare basalt, olivine phyric) - 0.27g
meteorites.path: Photos/Achondrites/Lunar/mare basalt/NWA 16286 (Lunar mare basalt, olivine phyric) - 0.27g
meteorites.description:
NWA 16286 (Lunar mare basalt, olivine phyric) - 0.27g
**NWA 16286** is an unbrecciated lunar **olivine-phyric mare basalt**, discovered in Northwest Africa in 2023. The official material consists of only three pieces with a combined mass of **311 g**. Petrographically, it contains zoned olivine phenocrysts set in a fine-grained basaltic groundmass of clinopyroxene and shock-transformed plagioclase (maskelynite), with abundant fine needles of ilmenite and minor chromite. Its bulk composition is unusual among lunar basalts: it is a **moderate-Ti, high-K basalt**, and it does not appear to be paired with any previously known basaltic lunar meteorite. ([sites.wustl.edu][1])

The most important discovery concerning NWA 16286 is its age. A 2025 Pb-Pb study determined a crystallization age of **2,201 ± 13 million years**, making it the **youngest known lunar meteorite**. This is particularly significant because lunar mare volcanism was thought to have become very limited by this stage of the Moon's history. Its geochemistry is also remarkable: the basalt has a strong **KREEP signature**, including a very high ^238U/^204Pb ratio of about 2000 and a negative εNd value. These characteristics indicate that its mantle source was substantially influenced by KREEP—the potassium-, rare-earth-element- and phosphorus-rich component produced during the Moon's early differentiation. ([ScienceDirect][2])

NWA 16286 therefore provides an important new constraint on how long the Moon remained volcanically active and how its interior continued to generate magma. Recent work suggests that KREEP may have played a **direct role in sustaining lunar magmatism much later than previously demonstrated**, extending evidence for KREEP-related volcanism by roughly 800 million years. Comparisons with the ~2.0-billion-year-old basalt returned by China's Chang'e 5 mission are especially revealing: although both are among the youngest lunar igneous samples and are enriched in rare-earth elements, only NWA 16286 shows clear evidence for direct KREEP involvement. The meteorite consequently offers a rare glimpse into the thermal and chemical evolution of the lunar mantle during the Moon's final major phase of basaltic volcanism. ([ScienceDirect][2])

[1]: https://sites.wustl.edu/meteoritesite/items/lm_nwa_16286/ "Lunar Meteorite: Northwest Africa 16286 | Some Meteorite Information | Washington University in St. Louis"
[2]: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2095927325008631 "2.2-billion-year-old KREEP-rich volcanism on the Moon - ScienceDirect"

From Yang Shun-Chung.

meteorites.name: NWA 14526 (Lunar mare basalt) - 4 fragments
meteorites.description:
NWA 14526 (Lunar mare basalt) - 4 fragments
**NWA 14526** is an unbrecciated lunar mare basalt found in Northwest Africa in 2021, with a total mass of about **505 grams**. It is a relatively fresh-looking, fine-grained basalt classified as **low-Ti, low-Al and low-K**, and contains minerals such as pyroxene, plagioclase (partly transformed to maskelynite by shock), olivine and phosphates. Radiometric dating places its crystallization at about **3.01 billion years ago**, making it a valuable sample of the Moon's later period of mare volcanism. Unlike many lunar meteorites, it is not heavily mixed or brecciated, so its minerals preserve a relatively clear record of the magma from which it crystallized. 

What makes NWA 14526 particularly interesting today is the **new isotopic work on its origin**. A 2025 study found that its source mantle was remarkably depleted in KREEP material, with the estimated KREEP contribution being less than **0.5%**. This is important because KREEP-rich material has often been invoked to explain why the Moon was still volcanically active relatively late in its history. NWA 14526 therefore provides evidence that **late lunar volcanism did not necessarily require a KREEP-enriched mantle source**. Its unusually high neodymium isotopic signature also distinguishes it from several superficially similar lunar basalts, meaning that despite their comparable ages and compositions, they are not genetically related. 

There is an especially nice new development here: a **2026 study** compared NWA 14526 with another lunar meteorite, **NWA 14992**, and concluded that the two probably represent a previously unrecognized paired group. Their similar mineralogy and chemistry record evidence for **magma recharge within the Moon around 3.0 billion years ago**—essentially, a younger, hotter batch of magma entering an existing magmatic system. This makes NWA 14526 more than simply a sample of an ancient lunar lava: it may preserve evidence of the **dynamic processes operating inside a lunar magma chamber during the Moon's prolonged period of late volcanism**. 

A gift from Matt Stream.

meteorites.name: NWA 8599 (Lunar Troctolitic breccia) - 20mg
meteorites.description:
NWA 8599 (Lunar Troctolitic breccia) - 20mg
**NWA 8599 is a particularly interesting piece of the Moon’s deep, magnesium-rich crust.** Recent work identifies it as an olivine-rich magnesian anorthositic noritic breccia containing fragments of unusually Mg-rich rocks. One small but remarkable fragment contains **very magnesian olivine (Fo84–87)** together with Mg-rich pyroxene and the mineral **geikielite**. The latter is the real headline: the 2025 study reported geikielite in NWA 8599 as the **first occurrence of this mineral in a lunar meteorite or any returned lunar sample**. ([geology.nju.edu.cn][1])

The mineral assemblage also provides clues about parts of the Moon that are poorly represented in the Apollo and Luna collections. The chemistry of the olivine and pyroxene suggests that this particular fragment originated from a **deep, Mg-rich region of the lunar crust**, rather than the shallow surface rocks that dominate our returned samples. The authors propose that the magnesian anorthosites in NWA 8599 may have formed through interaction between Mg-rich melts rising from the lunar mantle and the primordial ferroan anorthositic crust during **lunar mantle overturn**. In that sense, NWA 8599 may preserve a small piece of the deep lunar interior and evidence for the complicated mixing processes that helped construct the Moon’s early crust. ([geology.nju.edu.cn][1])

[1]: https://geology.nju.edu.cn/EN/abstract/abstract10486.shtml?utm_source=chatgpt.com "Petrography and Mineralogy of Lunar Magnesian Anorthositic Meteorite Northwest Africa 8599"

meteorites.name: Gadamis 003 (Lunar ferroan anorthosite) - 81mg
meteorites.description:
Gadamis 003 (Lunar ferroan anorthosite) - 81mg
"Apollo 16 Lunar"
**Gadamis 003 is scientifically interesting as an unusually pure sample of the Moon’s ancient anorthositic crust.** It is composed of roughly **98–99% anorthitic plagioclase**, with only tiny amounts of olivine and pyroxene enclosed within it. The mineral chemistry places it firmly within the **ferroan anorthosite (FAN) suite**, the rocks thought to represent products of the Moon’s primordial magma ocean. Its strongly cataclastic texture records intense fragmentation, while its exceptionally calcium-rich plagioclase is remarkably similar to ferroan anorthosite clasts returned by **Apollo 16**. In effect, Gadamis 003 is a piece of the ancient lunar crust that provides a useful comparison with the very limited Apollo sampling of the lunar highlands. ([LPI][1])

More recent research is beginning to make Gadamis 003 particularly interesting beyond its basic classification. A 2025 study of **Gadamis 003 and its related meteorite Gadamis 005** used high-resolution X-ray fluorescence mapping to investigate the chemical diversity of their anorthositic material and possible traces of **exogenous material introduced by impacts**. Another recent study has examined Gadamis 003's mineralogy and organic geochemistry, finding the expected anorthite, pyroxene and olivine together with accessory magnetite and ilmenite. Because Gadamis 003 belongs to a larger family of paired Gadamis meteorites, it may ultimately provide a particularly useful collection of samples for reconstructing the **composition, impact history and evolution of the Moon's ancient highland crust**. ([journals.lib.unb.ca][2])

[1]: https://www.lpi.usra.edu/meteor/metbull.cfm?code=75474&utm_source=chatgpt.com "Meteoritical Bulletin: Entry for Gadamis 003"
[2]: https://journals.lib.unb.ca/index.php/GC/article/download/34919/1882530895/1882544642?utm_source=chatgpt.com "Volume 52"

meteorites.description:
NWA 13916 (Polymict fragmental lunar breccia) - 1.9g
Electron microprobe analysis of a polished mount shows this meteorite to be a lunar polymict breccia with at least 9 distinct lithologies set in a fine-grained cataclastic groundmass of plagioclase, pyroxene and olivine fragments. Ubiquitous silica, merrillite, Fe-sulfide, Fe-metal (low Ni), and ilmenite were detected.

Clasts: (C. Agee, UNM) Groundmass olivine, clinopyroxene, n=13; plagioclase, n=5. Clast-1 (microgabbro) clinopyroxene, n=3; plagioclase, n=2. Clast-2 (ferroan anorthosite) olivine, n=1; clinopyroxene, n=1; plagioclase, n=1. Clast-3 (impact quench-crystal melt) olivine, n=1; clinopyroxene, n=2; plagioclase, n=1. Clast-4 (anorthositic gabbro) clinopyroxene, n=1; plagioclase, n=1. Clast-5 (troctolite) olivine, n=2; plagioclase n=2. Clast-6 (anorthositic troctolite) olivine, n=1; plagioclase, n=1. Clast-7 (microgabbro) clinopyroxene, n=1; plagioclase, n=1. Clast-8 (olivine microgabbro) olivine, n=1; clinopyroxene, n=1; plagioclase l, n=1. Clast-9 (lunar granite) alkali feldspar, n=2; silica polymorph.
Some notes from Dr. Agee on the colors of the minerals in this meteorite: The very white clasts are plagioclase. The light grays are a mixture of plagioclase, pyroxene, and olivine. The darker the gray, the finer the grain size. Very dark colors can also indicate the presence of shock melt. The orange spots could be fayalitic olivine. The white veins are desert carbonate filled cracks. Heavily shocked meteorites have lots of cracks and these are penetrated first by terrestrial weathering.

meteorites.name: NWA 5000 (lunar, fieldspathic breccia) - 0.446g
meteorites.description:
NWA 5000 (lunar, fieldspathic breccia) - 0.446g
"Legendary" lunar.

History: Found in July 2007 in southern Morocco and provided to Adam Hupé in October 2007.

We know from observation and the Apollo missions that there are two main classes of rocks from the moon. The first type is referred to as "mare" (meaning "sea"), pertaining to the darker areas of the moon mainly composed of ancient (3.0 to 3.8 billion year old) basalt lava flows. The second type referred to as "highlands" pertains to the lighter colored areas of the moon mainly composed of feldspar-rich anorthosite rocks. NWA 5000 is a unique highlands-monomict gabbroic breccia (meaning a type of rock mainly made of fragments of gabbro). The moon is believed to be about 4.5 billion years old and for about 600 million years during its early history was bombarded by pieces left over from formation of the planets. Impacts continued to pulverize the surface of the moon at a decreasing rate, creating the heavily cratered surface. During this time, melting of the lunar mantle produced basalt magma that erupted into the larger basins producing the dark areas of the moon, again referred to as "mare". Knowing this history of the moon, we know that NWA 5000 is ancient, making it older than most known Earth rocks.

The next period of NWA 5000’s existence was relatively quiet until a massive impact event occurring around 3.2 billion years ago created a giant melt sheet of a type of rock referred to as gabbro.  The impacting body left exotic 4.5 billion year old material in this Lunaite solving the mystery of why there is metal embedded in gabbro clasts (something that was never observed before NWA 5000 was studied.)  Another asteroid impact around 600 million years ago was mostly responsible for producing its distinctive brecciated matrix as well as bringing this rock to the surface of the moon.  This is where it was exposed to the solar wind, which implanted Helium 3 gas bubbles into the matrix. Then another impact event ejected this rock from the moon and created the interesting glass veins. According to ongoing studies, this happened around 2 thousand years ago.

Petrography: (A. Irving and S. Kuehner, UWS) Almost monomict fragmental breccia dominated by Mg-suite olivine gabbro clasts consisting predominantly of coarse-grained (0.5-2 mm) calcic plagioclase, pigeonite (some with fine exsolution lamellae), and olivine with accessory merrillite, Mg-bearing ilmenite, Ti-bearing chromite, baddeleyite, rare zirconolite, silica polymorph, K-feldspar, kamacite, and troilite. Some gabbro clasts have shock injection veins composed mostly of glass containing myriad fine troilite blebs and engulfed mineral fragments. Black, vitreous impact melt clasts consist of sporadic, small angular fragments (apparently surviving relics) of gabbro and related mineral phases in a very fine grained, non-vesicular, ophitic-textured matrix of pigeonite laths (up to 20 microns long × 2 microns wide) and interstitial plagioclase with tiny spherical grains of kamacite, irregular grains of schreibersite and rare troilite.

meteorites.description:
Tisserlitine 001 (feldspathic regolithic breccia, partially hydrothermally-altered) - 0.15g
Tisserlitine 001 may preserve evidence of an intriguing and still-debated process on the Moon: **alteration of lunar minerals by water**. Some of its olivine grains have been replaced by hydrated, clay-like minerals and iron oxides. At first, this was interpreted as possible hydrothermal alteration on the Moon, although terrestrial weathering is an obvious alternative explanation.

Recent studies have found several features that make a purely terrestrial origin less certain. The alteration is sometimes found deep within otherwise well-preserved rock, rather than along exposed surfaces or cracks, and occurs next to remarkably unaltered minerals that should also have been affected by terrestrial water. Hydrogen-isotope measurements, however, cannot yet distinguish lunar water from terrestrial water. **Tisserlitine 001 therefore remains an intriguing open question: did water alter these minerals on Earth, or could this meteorite preserve rare evidence that liquid water once interacted with rocks on the Moon?**

White crystals surrounding the tiny vugs are secondary calcite and the red crystals could be Cr-spinel.

meteorites.name: NWA 11788 (Lunar feldsp. breccia) - 0.36g
meteorites.description:
NWA 11788 (Lunar feldsp. breccia) - 0.36g
**NWA 11788 is particularly interesting because it appears to contain a remarkably diverse mixture of rocks from the lunar crust, including several lithologies related to the enigmatic lunar “Mg-suite.”** A detailed 2024 study found anorthositic norites, gabbros, troctolites and related rocks alongside more unusual basaltic material. The Mg-suite rocks are important because they formed from relatively magnesium-rich magmas within the Moon's crust, and their origin has long been difficult to reconcile with the simplest version of the lunar magma-ocean model. NWA 11788 shows striking similarities to rocks from the **Luna 20** collection and to the magnesian granulites returned by Apollo, suggesting that these seemingly disparate samples may represent related processes operating in the deeper lunar crust. ([Wiley Online Library][1])

Perhaps even more intriguing is the possibility that NWA 11788 can tell us **where on the Moon some of this material came from**. Its chemistry and mineralogy have been compared with the NWA 8673 clan, and researchers have suggested that the meteorite may represent material excavated from the deeper crust by a major impact. The possible source regions include areas around large impact basins, including the **South Pole–Aitken basin**—one of the largest and oldest impact structures in the Solar System. Work presented at the 2026 Lunar and Planetary Science Conference is now going further, investigating the ages and diversity of basalt and impact-melt clasts within NWA 11788. In other words, this meteorite isn't simply a piece of generic lunar highland rock: it may preserve a **fragmented geological record of the Moon's deep crust, ancient impacts, and magmatic evolution**, potentially from a region that has never been sampled directly by a lunar mission. ([hou.usra.edu][2])

[1]: https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/maps.14248 "Petrographic and geochemical analysis of lunar meteorite ..."
[2]: https://www.hou.usra.edu/meetings/lpsc2026/pdf/2025.pdf "2025.pdf 57th LPSC (2026)"

meteorites.name: NWA 6704 (achondrite-un) - 0.28g
meteorites.description:
NWA 6704 (achondrite-un) - 0.28g
NWA 6704 is an unusual, ungrouped basaltic achondrite meteorite that has a striking greenish-yellow color on the inside, and that is also relatively unaltered and un-shocked. The meteorite is coarse-grained with grain sizes around 1.5 millimeters, which is highly suggestive of a slow-cooling geologic environment. Matrix is overall medium grained with an igneous cumulate texture. Small grains of olivine (0.5-0.8 mm) and chromite (0.1-0.6 mm) enclosed within large (to 4 mm) orthopyroxene oikocrysts, which are in turn surrounded by large optically continuous, intercumulus grains of untwinned albite and <0.1 mm awaruite.The silicates contain curvilinear trains of tiny rounded inclusions (2-20 μm), which appear on polished surfaces to be empty bubbles with smooth rounded walls.
NWA 6704 could be one of the oldest rocks in the solar system, as multiple distinguished thermal events are revealed through U-Pb dating as well as Ar-Ar dating (American Astronomical Society, DPS meeting #49, 2017, id.110.23). The Re–Os isotope data for bulk and metal fractions yield an isochron age of 4576 ± 250 Ma, consistent with only limited open system behavior of highly siderophile elements (HSE) since formation.
NWA 6704 parent body sampled the same isotopic reservoirs in the solar nebula as the carbonaceous chondrite parent bodies.

meteorites.name: d'Orbigney (Angrite) - 81mg
meteorites.description:
d'Orbigney (Angrite) - 81mg
It was found near Buenos Aires, Argentina in September 1979. At 16.5kg it is the largest of only 12 angrite meteorites found to date.
No evidence of brecciation, shock metamorphism or significant thermal metamorphism are present. Some believe it might not have had ignious origin. 
It consists predominantly of Ca-bearing olivine and anorthite, which compose an intergrowth of plates and networks, as well as augite which likely formed later.
A late oxidizing event produced grains of the clinopyroxene Al,Ti–diopside-hedenbergite, which now fill most of the intergranular spaces. Large (up to 1 cm) clear to milky, green to greenish-white, magnesian olivine megacrysts and polycrystalline olivinites represent one of the earliest phases of the host rock. Also representing very early constituents, Cr-bearing Al-spinel and Fe-bearing spinel occur within some olivine and anorthite grains.

meteorites.description:
NWA 11220 (7034 paired) - "Black Beauty"
Martian (basaltic breccia)
NWA 7034 is a volcanic breccia that has a porphyritic appearance, consisting of plagioclase(andesine) and pyroxene (pigeonite and augite) phenocrysts that are up to 5 mm in diameter set in a fine grained groundmass. Accessory minerals include chlorapatite, chromite, goethite, ilmenite, magnetite, maghemite, alkali feldspar and pyrite.There are even some clasts present that are made of quenched magma. The groundmass is made from fine grained plagioclase, pyroxene, different oxide minerals, and traces of iron sulfides. The whole rock chemistry revealed that NWA 7034 has the highest water content ever measured in a Martian meteorite. The water might be derived from oceans that used to exist on Mars, but were still present when the volcanic rock, that would eventually become the meteorite, was erupted.

The meteorite contains components as old as 4.42 ± 0.07 Ga (billion years), and was heated during the Amazonian period of Mars. It is the second oldest Martian meteorite known. However, a team of Japanese researchers who studied the meteorite concluded that water on Mars originated around 4.4 billion years ago.

The melt inclusions contain rare amphiboles, and cracks within are filled with carbonate and sulfate salts, indicating a mild pre-terrestrial aqueous alteration.
Scientists found that unlike Chassigny, NWA 2737 has been hardly shocked, the pressure was so high that it turned the olivine black. Such a deformation in olivine has never been observed before.

It was originally documented as a basaltic shergottite because the pyroxene compositions and modal abundances are similar to Shergotty. However, recent work reclassified NWA 6963 as an intrusive, gabbroic Martian meteorite because of the large oriented pyroxene crystals.

NWA 12241 (olivine-gabbroic / poikilitic shergottite) - 20mg
It's one of the least shocked shergottites indicated by the lack of maskelynite, though with some thin shock veins (shock comparable to augite basalt find and nakhlites). Composed primarily of olivine and clinopyroxene with 15% (birefringent) plagioclase.  Accessory phases include Mg-merrillite, chlorapatite, ilmenite, Ti-rich chromite, Cr-rich chromite and pyrrhotite. 
It's possible it's been ejected from Mars in a separate ejection event than most other shergottites (samples a new, different location on Mars).

meteorites.description:

Two distinct pyroxene trends are present 1) Mg-rich low calcium pyroxene trending to slightly more Fe-rich pigeonite, 2) Mg-rich augite trending to more Ca-rich augite. Ilmenite, Fe-sulfide, and merrillite are minor ubiquitous phases.

Feldspar is a minor component and has completely been transformed to maskelynite. Accessory minerals include chomite, FeS and FeNiS. Contains glassy to finely recrystallized shock melt pocket.

meteorites.name: NWA 8159 (Martian augite basalt - 1-1)
meteorites.description:
NWA 8159 (Martian augite basalt - 1/1)
A gift from Eric Lyon.
With the TKW of 149.4g it's the rares of all the  Martian meteorite types.
Single stone, weathered exterior with yellow-brown patina, light colored desert soil coating on one side. Saw cut reveals a very fine-grained, gray-green interior, with a few small melt veins present, but one vein was up to 1 mm thick, lithology offsets at vein boundaries suggest slight brecciation.
Petrography: (C. Agee, UNM) Microprobe examination of a two polished mounts shows intergranular texture with approximately 50% augite, 40% plagioclase and maskelynite, 5% olivine. Augites have equant habits 10-200 μm with igneous zoning. Some augite crystals are rimmed with Fs-rich orthopyroxene. Plagioclase with shock-fractured prismatic laths up to 500 × 100 μm, but many are smaller (~50 × 10 μm), approximately half of the plagioclase has been converted to maskelynite, and is observed as unfractured, glassy casts. Olivine ~100 μm, most with resorbed or coronal grain boundaries. Ubiquitous magnetite, most grains 10-100 μm. Minor ilmenite, merrillite, Cl-apatite, and Cr-spinel. Trace calcite and barite assumed to be desert weathering products.

meteorites.name: NWA 15200 (nakhlite) - 171mg

NWA 15200 (nakhlite) - 171mg
The "200g nakhlite".

This meteorite is an augite-rich cumulate rock with ferro-hypersthene, fayalitic olivine, andesine plagioclase, Al-K-rich mesostasis, Ti-Cr magnetite, ilmenite, and troilite. Augite grains can be more than millimeter in size, as are the olivine grains. Augite is weakly zoned. Ferro-hypersthene commonly occurs as a separate phase, but also as ferroan rims on some augite grains. Olivines are relatively uniform in composition with no igneous zoning present. Plagioclase and mesostasis typically occupy interstitial spaces between larger pyroxene and olivine grains. Maskelynite is absent.

meteorites.name: NWA 15364 (nakhlite) - 0.228g
meteorites.description:
NWA 15364 (nakhlite) - 0.228g

Outer margins of augite grains contain orthopyroxene and pigeonite, and some augite occurs as stubby inclusions within olivine. Intercumulus regions contain fine grained, apparently hydrous "chlorophaeite" (red-brown in thin section), and similar material is present as thin veinlets within olivine grains.

Petrography: (C. Agee, UNM) This meteorite has an ophitic texture consisting of 75% augite, 15% feldspar, and 5% olivine. Some augite crystals are prismatic and up to 2 mm in length. There are two feldspars present, oligoclase and alkali feldspar, no maskelynite was observed; feldspar commonly occupies interstices between augite grains. Augites show igneous zoning with Fs-rich rims, olivines are fayalitic and fairly uniform in composition. Apatite, ilmenite, and titanomagnetite were observed.

meteorites.description:
Dhofar 007 (Eucrite-Cumulate) - 1.09g
Dhofar 007 is composed by equal proportion of anorthite (the Ca-rich pole of plagioclase) and clinopyroxenes (augite and pigeonite), with minor amounts of free nicekl-iron, chromite and phosphates.

Formed by fractional crystallization of a magma with peridititic composition, this cumulate eucrite was slowly cooled in the crust of its parent body (probably Vesta). The depht of the magma chamber, based on the augite lamellae widht and Ca zoning proflies, is estimated to 7-8km...

Dhofar 007 has experienced a two-stage postcrystallization thermal history: rapid cooling at high temperatures and slow cooling at lower temperatures. The slow cooling rate is comparable to those in mesosiderites and pallasites. The two-stage thermal history and the relative abundance of siderophile elements similar to those for metallic portions in mesosiderites suggest that Dhofar 007 could be a large inclusion of mesosiderite, or can suggest that Dhofar 007 is an anomalous eucrite.

meteorites.name: Maslyanino (iron, IAB complex) - 4.74g
meteorites.description:
Maslyanino (iron, IAB complex) - 4.74g
The meteorite is a fine-structural octahedrite. Its metallic matrix consists of kamacite, taenite, and schreibersite. Large troilite segregations are associated with silicate inclusions; in addition, rare minerals altaite and dobreelite are found. The silicate inclusions contain olivine, orthopyroxene, clinopyroxene, plagioclase, apatite, merrillite, chromite, and graphite. A detailed trace-element analysis of the metallic matrix permits the Maslyanino meteorite to be assigned to the narrow Pitts subgroup of the IAB group. It is also similar to meteorites of the Udei Station subgroup. The data obtained are consistent with the formation of the meteoritic material under impact of a parent asteroid resulting in the removal of its outer chondrite–winonaite shell. Subsequent weaker impacts led to the formation of IAB group meteorites (including meteorites with silicate inclusions) and winonaites from the asteroid remnant.

It is said that one of local nobelman, perhaps Puta von Illburk, was cursed by an old woman, struck by lightning and transformed into this hard piece of iron. In those days, superstition also had that the Elbogen meteorite was fixed with chains in the dungeon of the Loket castle for fear that it would change weight over time, and even is thrown into the deep castle well that it would always reappear. During the Thirty Years' War the royal and imperial general Johann von Werth decided to try this out by having it thrown into the castle well. However, by the end of 1670 the water in the well was drawn off and the stone was pulled out and brought into the castle. In 1742, the French threw the rock back into the well and it stayed there until sometime in 1776 when it was once more recovered.

AGUAS ZARCAS (CM2 W0) - 0.34g

Stones are brecciated and dominated by two lithologies: chondrule poor, constituting ~80 areal% of the broken surfaces examined (~2 kg of material), and chondrule rich. Chondrules constitute ~10 areal% of the chondrule-poor lithology and ~40 areal% in the chondrule-rich lithology.  A probe mount of the dominant chondrule-poor lithology (sample area 1.5 × 2.2 cm) shows scattered small chondrules (mean 275 μm, n=40), with prominent fine-grained rims. Rare chondrules to 2 mm. Fe-Ni metal, which is Cr-bearing, was only found as rounded grains in one 100-μm type I chondrule. The section contains several Al-rich CAIs to 300 μm. The matrix is dominated by two components of roughly equal proportions: anhedral clumps (typically 50 microns) that are Fe and S rich (e.g., 37.5 wt% Fe and 5.8 wt% S, with microprobe total of 93%), surrounded by fine-grained material poorer in Fe and S (e.g., 12.8 wt% Fe, 13.9 wt% Mg, and 0.5 wt% S, with microprobe total of 80.0%). Powder XRD from five stones (one chondrule rich) shows patterns dominated by serpentine. In two stones, the serpentine 001 reflection sits on a broad peak centered at 0.843 nm. Reflections for tochilinite and calcite occur in all patterns. The intensities of olivine and pyroxene reflections were generally low, but most prominent in the chondrules-rich stone.

meteorites.name: TAGISH LAKE (C2-un S1 W0) - 25mg
meteorites.description:
TAGISH LAKE (C2-un S1 W0) - 25mg
British Columbia, Canada
Fell 2000 January 18 over the Yukon Territory and northern British Columbia. Jim Brook recovered several dozen meteorites totaling ~ 1 kg on the ice of Taku Arm, Tagish Lake, on January 25 and 26 (coordinates of first find given above).  Between April 20 and May 8, ~ 500 additional specimens were located on the ice of Taku Arm and a small, unnamed lake 1.5 km to the east, but only ~ 200 were retrieved as many had melted down into the ice making their collection time consuming; recovery was prioritized based on meteorites' mass and degree of disaggregation.  The total mass collected was between 5 and 10 kg. Classification and mineralogy (M. Zolensky, JSC; M. Grady, NHM):  possibly CI2 group; a matrix-dominated chondrite, with a few small chondrules, CAIs, and isolated grains; matrix mainly phyllosilicates, Fe-Ni sulfides and magnetite, with abundant Ca-Mg-Fe carbonates;
Tagish Lake meteorite shows isotopic anomalies indicative of mass fractionation during chemical reactions at extremely low temperatures (10 to 20 kelvin), characteristic of cold molecular clouds and the outer protosolar disk. The globules probably originated as organic ice coatings on preexisting grains that were photochemically processed into refractory organic matter. The globules resemble cometary carbon, hydrogen, oxygen, and nitrogen (CHON) particles, suggesting that such grains were important constituents of the solar system starting materials.

Contains more presolar nano diamonds than any other meteorite.

meteorites.description:
Tarda (C2-ung, S-low W0) - 57mg
25 August 2020, Moroccan fall.
Hundreds of small to medium-sized fusion crusted stones ranging from 0.1 g to 99 g. The majority of the fusion-crusted stones are <1 g. Some flight-oriented stones show a blue iridescence on their trailing edge, similar to that observed with Aguas Zarcas. Many stones shattered upon impact with the ground. The stones have low density, are somewhat friable, and are particularly susceptible to moisture, and rapidly slake in contact with water or alcohol. 
The bulk mineralogy is consistent with a petrologic grade 2, based on the predominance of smectite and serpentine together with the presence of anhydrous mafic silicates, AOA, and chondrules. The oxygen isotopes give a bimodal distribution of the δ18O-values, with one group having values somewhat like those of the CI chondrites, and the other group like values for the Yamato-type (CY) carbonaceous chondrites (King et al., 2019). However, Δ17O values are lower than those for CI and CY chondrites, and plot below the TFL. These isotopic values do not overlap with those of any established carbonaceous chondrite group, hence the ungrouped designation.

meteorites.name: ISHEYEVO (CH-CBb) - 0.5g
meteorites.description:
ISHEYEVO (CH/CBb) - 0.5g
As the only meteorite with a CH/CB classification Isheyevo (tkw 16kg) exhibits mineralogical characteristics intermediate between CH and CBb.
Isheyevo consists primarily of two lithologies that transition smoothly between each another—one lithology that is metal-rich and most similar to the CBb chondrites, and another that is metal-poor and most similar to the CH3 chondrites. Compared to the metal-poor lithology, which contains up to 90 vol% chondrules measuring 0.2–1 mm, the metal-rich lithology contains a significantly lower abundance of chondrules, as low as 30 vol%, measuring 0.1–0.4 mm. Moreover, the metal-rich lithology contains a greater percentage of non-porphyritic chondrules compared to the metal-poor lithology, and also contains six times the abundance of highly refractory CAIs (Ivanova et al., 2006). The majority population (~55%) of CAIs have igneous textures and show little interaction with a cooling nebula gas. These CAIs were isolated from the hot nebula region and experienced rapid cooling. This is a distinct population of CAIs compared to those found in all other carbonaceous chondrite groups.

Aba Panu meteorite fell in Nigeria on April 19, 2018. The event was reported to the local residents as an earthquake, but in reality it was a meteor fragmentation event in the atmosphere that got everyone’s attention. The total known weight is ~170kg, with 100kg appropriated by the government.

Petrography: Visually the cut surfaces are dominated by a gray matrix, studded with well-developed chondrules and chondrule fragments. Some chondrules to 4 mm but the majority are 0.1 to 1 mm across. Observations on an 8 × 7 cm slab shows the following clasts: L6 (3 × 1 cm); L5 (1.5 × 1 cm); and sub-rounded 1-cm dark clast with sparse 200 micron chondrules. Shock veins are rare. Metal and sulfide occurs as: fined grained spheres in the matrix; armoring chondrules; and, occasional lumps to 5 mm. Petrographic observations show a range of chondrule types dominated by PO, POP, RP, PP, and BO. Particularly evident in thin section are BO and PO chondrules with reddish purple (in plain polarized light) glass that is isotropic under crossed polars. The silicates are extensively shocked with olivine showing mosaicism and PDFs. SEM observations show that much of the metal/sulfide in the matrix occurs as fine-droplets, veins, and melt pods. Large Fe-Ni grains are polycrystalline with each crystal showing a kamacite core, dark-etched martensitic inner rim, and outer Ni-rich rim. Troilite is dominantly single crystal, and occasionally polycrystalline. Sparse chromite grains.

Range of chondrule types, though largely recrystallized and integrated with the matrix, the chondrules still recognizable including a large BO (to 5 mm), PO and PP. Feldspar shows a range of sizes, some grains to 200 μm, though majority <50 μm. Metal and troilite heterogeneously distributed across the mount, largest grains to 100 μm. A few small melt pockets observed in the mount are consistent with shock stage S3 .

meteorites.description:
CHELYABINSK (LL5 S4 W0) - 0.72g

On February 15, 2013, a bright fireball was seen by numerous residents and a shower of stones fell ~40 km S of Chelyabinsk (100kg). The majority (2/3) of the stones are composed of a light-colored lithology with a typical chondritic texture. Chondrules (~63%, mean 0.93mm) are readily delineated and set within a fragmental matrix. The chondrule glass is devitrified. The main phases are olivine and orthopyroxene. Olivine shows mosaicism and planar fractures. Rare grains of augite and clinobronzite are present.  Troilite (4 vol.%) and FeNi metal (1.3 vol.%) occur as irregularly shaped grains. A significant portion (1/3) of the stones consist of a dark, fine-grained impact melt containing mineral and chondrule fragments. Feldspar is well developed and practically isotropic. There are black-colored thin shock veins in both light and dark lithologies.

Mount Baldr A76002 (H6) - micro
The second find of the first joined USA/Japanese Antarctic expedition.
From Bill Cassidy's book:
At the top was a small patch of exposed ice about 3 × 3km in area, partially covered in a very patchy way by snow. It didn’t look very promising, but we got out and Keizo almost immediatedly spotted a meteorite near the helo. We were ecstatic, but while we were photographing it and admiring it, Keizo was scanning the ice with his binoculars. Presently he started running and we, of course, followed. Sam ran back to the helicopter and took off, following us at an elevation of about 2m, and 20m behind. In silhouette, it would have been a memorable, if puzzling, tableau: a figure running at top speed over the ice, two more people chasing him and a helicopter skimming along behind. I remember looking back and thinking that this is what an insect must feel like, being stalked by a praying mantis. Meanwhile, Keizo had spotted another meteorite. So Keizo Yanai had found our first two meteorites during our
first 20 minutes in the field, and that is how it all began. We didn’t find another for the next six weeks!
